name: Sweden
summary_text: Sweden is very safe. A new Legal Gender Recognition Act (July 2025) simplified the procedure and separated it from surgery requirements, but it still falls short of self-determination — a medical examination and a decision by the National Board of Health and Welfare are required. Sweden was the last Nordic country to reform its 1972-era LGR law. One documented axis-C friction: the Medley swimming-pool company's national guidelines restrict trans persons' changing-room access — lawyers say this may violate discrimination law. Brå (the crime-prevention council) reports roughly 6,700 LGBTQI-related hate-crime reports, and the government is mapping digital threats against LGBTQI individuals. There are no documented severe incidents (no tourist-rape, mob violence, or Pride-terrorism equivalent to Norway's Oslo shooting). Bathrooms as such are unrestricted, and there is no criminalisation or rollback movement.

sources.claim_summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry (April 2024) covers Sweden's parliament approving new acts on legal gender and medical procedures performed on genitalia.

sources.title: Swedish gender recognition law takes effect, but medical barriers remain - TGEU - Trans Europe and Central AsiaTGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia
sources.claim_summary: TGEU (July 2025): Sweden's new Legal Gender Recognition Act took effect 1 July 2025 - it simplifies the procedure (digital healthcare consultations, age limit lowered to 16, parental consent under 16) but falls short of self-determination: a medical examination and a National Board of Health and Welfare decision are still required, continuing to pathologise trans people; the Christian Democrats and right-wing opposition vow to reverse it.

sources.title: Simhallsjätten Medley: Därför får transpersoner inte välja omklädningsrum | SVT Nyheter
sources.claim_summary: SVT (Oct 2025, in Swedish): swimming-pool giant Medley stops trans people from choosing changing rooms - the company motivates its policy as being 'for all visitors to feel safe', a policy affecting trans swimmers' access to facilities.

sources.title: Persons suspected of offences with LGBTQI-related hate crimes | Brå - Brottsförebyggande rådet
sources.claim_summary: Brå (Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention) report 2024:13 summary: 'Persons suspected of offences with LGBTQI-related hate crimes' - descriptive analysis of suspects in reported offences with identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives, supplementing Sweden's hate-crime statistics.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Sweden: Stockholm's second LGBTI senior residence opened; the Migration Agency was instructed to improve consistency in LGBTI asylum claims and conversion-practices cases, though RFSL reports continued reliance on stereotypical credibility assessments; asylum and migration legislation tightening, with concerns it may disproportionately affect LGBTI asylum seekers.

sources.title: LGBT in the Military: Policy Development in Sweden 1944–2014 | Sexuality Research and Social Policy | Springer Nature Link
sources.claim_summary: Sundevall & Persson, 'LGBT in the Military: Policy Development in Sweden 1944-2014' (Sexuality Research and Social Policy, 2016): archival study of Swedish Armed Forces LGBT policy - two 'turns' (1971-79, when homosexuality was classified as mental illness and framed as a security/blackmail risk, and 2000-09, shifting focus to organisational structures); no formal ban ever existed.

sources.title: Canada, Portugal, Sweden Named World’s Most LGBTQ-Friendly Travel Destinations - Newsweek
sources.claim_summary: Newsweek (2019): Canada, Portugal and Sweden tied as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations in the Spartacus Gay Travel Index - Sweden's top-tier ranking for LGBT travellers.

sources.title: Sweden to stop calling transgender people 'mentally ill'
sources.claim_summary: The Local (Jan 2017): Sweden to stop classifying transgender people as 'mentally ill' - the National Board of Health and Welfare (Socialstyrelsen) announced the change, widely criticised as overdue.
